title: Malaysia | BNM Fair Treatment of Financial Consumers and Complaints
tagline: Treat customers fairly the Malaysian way: FTFC outcomes, honest disclosure, no prohibited conduct, fast complaints and airtight secrecy.
sectors: Bancassurance and wealth sales teams in banks
description:
A Malaysia-specific conduct quest for staff of conventional licensed banks. It is based on the **Financial Services Act 2013** (sections 123, 124, 126, 133 and 134 and Schedules 7 and 11) and the Bank Negara Malaysia (BNM) policy documents on **Fair Treatment of Financial Consumers** (2024, with vulnerable consumer rules from 1 April 2025), **Product Transparency and Disclosure** (2024), **Prohibited Business Conduct** (2016), **Complaints Handling** (in force from 1 April 2026) and **Management of Customer Information and Permitted Disclosures** (2025), with referral to the **Financial Markets Ombudsman Service**.

These documents require banks to train staff, representatives and agents on the conduct needed for fair outcomes, to train sellers on disclosure, complaints staff on complaints procedures, frontline staff on vulnerable consumers, and all staff on customer information confidentiality. This quest supports those duties for frontline, sales, product, complaints and management staff, and uses a real BNM enforcement case on customer information.

It builds knowledge of the Malaysian framework and does not replace your bank's own policies, procedures or role-specific training. Islamic banking requirements are outside its scope.
audience: Branch, contact-centre and digital banking staff who serve individual and small business customers in Malaysia
Personal bankers, relationship managers and bancassurance staff who advise on and sell products
Product, marketing and disclosure teams who design products, PDS documents and advertisements
Complaints handling officers and customer experience teams
Managers and senior officers accountable for conduct, complaints and customer information
outcomes: Explain the FSA basis of BNM's conduct standards and the seven FTFC outcomes
Apply the Product Transparency and Disclosure rules, including the PDS, digital disclosure and marketing consent
Recognise the six prohibited business conduct practices and give suitable, affordable advice
Identify and respond to vulnerable consumers in line with FTFC Principle 7
Handle complaints within BNM's turnaround times and refer customers to FMOS or BNMLINK
Protect customer information under FSA section 133 and the MCIPD policy document, and escalate breaches

quest.name: The Pelangi Promise
quest.premise: You have just joined the Consumer Conduct team of Pelangi Utama Bank Berhad, a fictional conventional bank headquartered in Kuala Lumpur with branches in Ipoh, Johor Bahru and Penang. BNM's conduct supervisors arrive in five weeks. With your mentor Nurul Aina, banker Arif, complaints lead Kavitha, branch manager Daniel and product manager Grace, clear five stages from the Charter Hall to the Vault Room, then face the final boss: the supervisors' questions.

badge.name: Fair Treatment Champion (MY)
badge.description: Awarded to bank staff who can apply BNM's fair treatment, disclosure, complaints and customer information rules with confidence.

cast.name: Nurul Aina Ismail
cast.role: Head of Consumer Conduct, your mentor

sessions.title: The FTFC Framework: Outcomes, Culture and Your Training Duty
sessions.summary: Where Malaysia's fair treatment rules come from: the Financial Services Act, BNM's 2024 Fair Treatment of Financial Consumers policy document, its seven outcomes, the Treat Customers Fairly Charter, and the culture, pay and training duties that make fairness real.
objectives: Explain how FSA section 123 lets BNM set binding business conduct standards for banks
Name the seven fair treatment outcomes and link each to everyday bank work
Distinguish an S standard from G guidance and say why the difference matters
Describe the Board, senior management and staff roles in an FTFC culture, including training under paragraphs 10.6 and 10.7

cards.title: Monday at Pelangi Utama
cards.setting: Consumer Conduct office, Pelangi Utama Bank Berhad, Kuala Lumpur. Monday, 8:45 am.

lines.text: Your access card still smells of new plastic when Nurul Aina waves you into the Consumer Conduct office on the 18th floor.
Welcome to Consumer Conduct. I'm Nurul Aina, and I'm your mentor for this quest. BNM's conduct supervisors arrive in five weeks to look at how we treat customers.
Arif here, from personal banking in Ipoh. Quick question before your coffee: my branch team is chasing a sales campaign. Is that a problem?
It might be. Kavitha, Complaints. Last quarter half our complaints on that product said nobody explained the lock-in fee.
That's the tension we live with. Selling is fine. Selling in a way that leaves customers worse off is a conduct risk, and BNM treats it seriously.
Stage 1 is the foundation: which law, which policy document, which outcomes, and who must do what. Ready?

scenes.heading: Financial Services Act 2013
scenes.narration: Section 123 of the Financial Services Act lets Bank Negara Malaysia set business conduct standards so that banks are fair, responsible and professional with financial consumers.

scenes.heading: The FTFC policy document
scenes.narration: BNM used that power for the Fair Treatment of Financial Consumers policy document, issued on 27 March 2024. It replaced the 2019 version and applies to licensed banks.

scenes.heading: A family of documents
scenes.narration: FTFC sits beside other BNM conduct documents: Product Transparency and Disclosure, Prohibited Business Conduct, Complaints Handling, and Management of Customer Information and Permitted Disclosures.

scenes.heading: Prohibited conduct
scenes.narration: Section 124 and Schedule 7 of the Act go further: they list practices a bank must never engage in, such as misleading customers or pressuring them.

scenes.heading: Who enforces
scenes.narration: BNM supervises conduct and can take enforcement action. Customers who stay unhappy can go to the Financial Markets Ombudsman Service, the approved ombudsman scheme.

cards.title: From statute to your desk
cards.caption: Each layer depends on the one above. When BNM inspects, it follows the chain all the way down to individual customer files.

items.label: FSA 2013, section 123
items.detail: Gives BNM the power to set conduct standards for financial service providers.

items.label: BNM policy documents
items.detail: FTFC, Product Transparency and Disclosure, Complaints Handling and others turn the power into rules.

items.label: Bank policies
items.detail: The Board approves policies; senior management builds processes, training and controls.

items.label: Your daily conduct
items.detail: Every explanation, recommendation and complaint reply is where the outcomes are won or lost.

cards.question: Under which provision does BNM specify the FTFC requirements for licensed banks?
options: Section 133 of the Financial Services Act 2013, which deals with customer secrecy
Section 123 of the Financial Services Act 2013, which lets BNM set business conduct standards
The Persons with Disabilities Act 2008, which BNM administers for banks
cards.explanation: The FTFC document cites sections 121 and 123 of the FSA for its requirements. Section 133 is the secrecy rule, and BNM does not administer the disability law.

cards.title: The seven FTFC outcomes
cards.body:
Paragraph 8.1 says a bank must apply the policy document to deliver **seven outcomes** for financial consumers:

1. **Culture**: confidence that fair treatment and their best interests are part of the bank's culture and core values.
2. **No unfair discrimination**, including no unfair contract terms that significantly disadvantage them.
3. **Clear, relevant, timely information** before, during and after the sale, including costs, risks and key exclusions.
4. **Due care, skill and diligence** from staff, representatives and agents.
5. **Suitable advice** that fits their financial needs and circumstances.
6. **Prompt, fair and effective** handling of complaints and claims.
7. **Vulnerable consumers treated fairly and equitably** (this seventh outcome applied from **1 April 2025**).

Think of them as the test BNM applies to everything else in the document.

cards.title: Match the outcome to the moment
cards.prompt: Link each everyday situation to the FTFC outcome it tests most directly.

pairs.right: A customer receives the fee table and risk warnings before she signs, not after.
A banker checks a retiree's goals and risk appetite before recommending anything.
A complaint about a wrong charge is acknowledged, investigated and answered on time.
A loan is not refused simply because of the applicant's race or religion.
A customer with hearing loss is offered a channel that works for him.

lines.text: Grace Wong, Products and Disclosure. I keep hearing 'BNM says' about things that are only good practice. How do you tell?
Look at the margin. Paragraphs marked S are standards: they must be complied with, and breaches can lead to enforcement action.
Paragraphs marked G are guidance: they explain and recommend. The good and poor practice boxes are examples, not extra rules.
So if guidance suggests an annual refresher, that's optional?
The method is flexible. The standard behind it is not. If paragraph 10.6 says staff must be trained, you still have to prove the training happened and worked.

cards.title: FTFC words you will hear all week

cards.back: Anyone who uses, has used or may use a financial product for personal, domestic or household purposes, plus micro and small businesses as BNM specifies.
Risk that the bank's business conduct leads to poor outcomes for consumers and harms the bank's reputation or finances.
A requirement that must be complied with. Non-compliance may lead to enforcement action.
Explanation or recommendation that BNM encourages banks to adopt.
Employees, including temporary or contract staff whose conduct affects consumer outcomes, even without direct customer contact.
Individuals or firms acting for the bank, such as sales representatives and bancassurance staff.

cards.title: Who owns fair treatment
cards.caption: Paragraph 10.2 sets the Board's role, 10.3 makes senior management primarily responsible, and 10.6 requires everyone delivering outcomes to be trained.

items.label: Board: tone from the top
items.detail: Promotes a sound culture, shows commitment, approves FTFC policies and checks strategy reflects them.

items.label: Senior management: drives the agenda
items.detail: Embeds FTFC in business model, product life cycle, recruitment, training, appraisal and rewards.

items.label: Staff, representatives, agents
items.detail: Deliver the outcomes in every conversation, document and decision.

cards.title: The campaign leaderboard
cards.situation: Arif's regional head wants to launch a 'Top Seller' leaderboard for a personal loan campaign. Bonuses would be paid purely on the ringgit value each banker sells in six weeks. Arif asks you whether this fits BNM's expectations on performance measures and pay.

choices.text: Suggest balancing the scorecard with qualitative criteria such as suitability, file quality and customer feedback, and flag the design to Consumer Conduct before launch.
choices.outcome: Paragraph 10.8 requires performance measures to include qualitative criteria that reflect FTFC outcomes, and 10.11 asks for sufficient weight on them. Raising it before launch is the cheapest fix.

choices.text: Approve it, because sales targets are a normal business decision outside BNM's conduct rules.
choices.outcome: Incorrect. FTFC paragraphs 10.8 to 10.11 bring performance measures and variable pay squarely into conduct rules.

choices.text: Approve it, but remind bankers verbally to be fair to customers.
choices.outcome: A reminder helps a little, but the incentive design still rewards volume only, which the policy document lists as a poor practice.

cards.title: Pay that helps or hurts
cards.caption: Paragraphs 10.10 and 10.11 require remuneration to be aligned with FTFC outcomes and variable pay to give enough weight to qualitative criteria.

items.label: Measure
items.right: Volume plus suitability and file quality

cards.title: Building the training duty
cards.prompt: Put the steps senior management follows to meet the FTFC training duty in a sensible order.
steps: Set and communicate the core values and desired behaviour needed to deliver fair outcomes
Identify each role's touchpoints across the product life cycle
Design role-specific training that shows how the FTFC principles apply at each stage
Deliver training to staff, representatives and agents and record completion
Monitor outcomes and staff performance against qualitative criteria
Refresh training and correct practices where outcomes are not met

cards.question: Paragraph 10.7 of the FTFC policy document describes what the training under paragraph 10.6 should look like. Which description fits best?
options: One identical e-learning module for all employees, repeated each year with the same questions
A legal briefing on the Financial Services Act for senior management only, delivered on appointment
Specific to each person's role, covering how FTFC applies across the product life cycle and the bank's core values
cards.explanation: Paragraph 10.6 (a standard) requires training on core values and desired conduct. Paragraph 10.7 (guidance) says it should be role-specific and cover the product life cycle. A single generic module misses that.

cards.title: Pelangi Utama's Treat Customers Fairly Charter
Stage 1 takeaways
items: FSA section 123 lets BNM set binding conduct standards; the 2024 FTFC policy document is the core one for fair treatment.
Seven outcomes are the yardstick, with the vulnerable consumer outcome applying from 1 April 2025.
S paragraphs must be complied with; G paragraphs guide how.
The Board sets the tone, senior management drives FTFC, and pay and performance measures must reward good conduct.
Staff, representatives and agents must be trained on core values and desired conduct, ideally role by role across the product life cycle.

cards.prompt: Think of one product you handle. At which stage of its life cycle (design, promotion, sale, advice, after-sales) is your role most likely to make or break a fair outcome, and what would good conduct look like there?

quiz.question: Which statement best describes the legal basis of BNM's Fair Treatment of Financial Consumers policy document for a licensed bank?
options: It is a voluntary industry code agreed by banks and the Securities Commission
It sets standards under the Financial Services Act 2013, including section 123 on business conduct
It is guidance only, so no part of it can lead to enforcement action
It is made under the Personal Data Protection Act 2010 for consumer data
quiz.explanation: The document cites FSA sections 121 and 123 for its standards. Its S paragraphs are binding and non-compliance may lead to enforcement; it is not a voluntary code or a data protection instrument.

quiz.question: From which date did the FTFC requirements on vulnerable consumers, including Outcome 7, take effect?
options: 6 November 2019
27 March 2024
1 April 2026
1 April 2025
quiz.explanation: The policy document took effect on 27 March 2024, but paragraph 4.1 deferred Outcome 7, paragraphs 10.3(f) and (g), 10.4 and 16.1 to 16.28 to 1 April 2025. 1 April 2026 is the Complaints Handling start date.

quiz.question: A sole proprietor running a micro business opens a business current account at your branch. Is she a 'financial consumer' for FTFC purposes?
options: Yes, because BNM specifies micro and small businesses as financial consumers
Only if the account is opened online rather than at a branch
Only if the business has a turnover above the SME threshold
No, because only individuals acting for household purposes are covered
quiz.explanation: Paragraph 7.1 covers personal, domestic or household use and also persons using products in connection with a micro or small business. The channel and a minimum turnover are irrelevant.

quiz.question: Your bank's code of ethics is strong, but no one has been told how it applies to selling credit cards. Under FTFC, what is missing?
options: A Securities Commission licence for each credit card salesperson
A public statement that credit cards are excluded from the FTFC charter
Training on core values and desired conduct that is specific to the role and product stage
A separate Board resolution approving the credit card product terms
quiz.explanation: Paragraph 10.6 requires training on core values and desired conduct, and 10.7 says it should be role-specific and cover the product life cycle. The policy document lists the lack of specific guidance to staff as a poor practice.

quiz.question: A sales head proposes paying bonuses based only on ringgit volume sold. Which FTFC requirement is most directly at risk?
options: The Treat Customers Fairly Charter must be published on the website
Performance measures must include qualitative criteria that reflect fair outcomes
Promotional materials must carry warnings that are not obscured
Complaints must be acknowledged in writing on the next working day
quiz.explanation: Paragraph 10.8 requires qualitative criteria alongside quantitative targets, and 10.11 requires sufficient weight on them for variable pay. The other options are real duties but are not what a volume-only bonus breaches.

quiz.question: Which person carries primary responsibility for driving the FTFC agenda and embedding it in the bank's culture?
options: Each branch manager individually
The Financial Markets Ombudsman Service
The Board's audit committee only
Senior management
quiz.explanation: Paragraph 10.3 makes senior management primarily responsible for driving FTFC, while the Board sets the tone from the top under 10.2. FMOS resolves disputes; it does not run the bank's culture.

quiz.question: A temporary contract worker in the back office processes loan documents but never meets customers. Is he within the FTFC meaning of 'staff'?
options: No, because only customer-facing roles are covered
Yes, if his conduct can affect consumer outcomes, even without direct contact
Only once he has completed six months of service
No, because only permanent employees count as staff
quiz.explanation: The FTFC definition of staff includes temporary or contract staff whose conduct affects consumer outcomes, whether or not they deal directly with customers.

quiz.question: A colleague says a paragraph marked 'G' in the FTFC document can be ignored. What is the best reply?
options: G paragraphs only apply to insurers and do not concern banks
G paragraphs replace the S paragraphs whenever the two seem to differ
G paragraphs are guidance that BNM encourages; they explain how to meet the binding S standards
G paragraphs are binding standards and every breach is a criminal offence
quiz.explanation: S marks standards that must be complied with; G marks guidance and recommendations that banks are encouraged to adopt. Guidance does not override standards, and it applies to banks too.

quiz.question: What must a bank publish prominently on its website under paragraph 9.1 of the FTFC policy document?
options: The minutes of Board meetings discussing conduct risk
Its commitment to treating consumers fairly and how it intends to implement it
Its full internal remuneration policy for sales staff
A list of complaints made by named customers in the past year
quiz.explanation: Paragraph 9.1 requires the commitment and its implementation, often as a Treat Customers Fairly Charter. Pay policies and Board minutes are internal, and customer names would breach secrecy.

quiz.question: Which of these is part of senior management's FTFC role under paragraph 10.3?
options: Approving each individual customer's loan application personally
Deciding disputes that customers refer to the ombudsman scheme
Aligning recruitment, training, appraisals and rewards with the desired values and outcomes
Issuing binding conduct standards to other financial institutions
quiz.explanation: Paragraph 10.3(h) lists aligning recruitment, training, appraisals and rewards. Individual credit decisions are delegated, ombudsman disputes are decided by FMOS, and only BNM issues standards.

sessions.title: Telling It Straight: Product Transparency, Disclosure and Fair Terms
sessions.summary: BNM's December 2024 Product Transparency and Disclosure policy document and the FTFC rules on fair terms: the five disclosure principles, the three stages of disclosure, the Product Disclosure Sheet, digital disclosure, advertising, consent for marketing and the training duty for those who sell.
objectives: Apply the five key disclosure principles and the three stages of disclosure to a bank product
State the main Product Disclosure Sheet rules, including length, timing and digital display
Recognise misleading advertising, pre-ticked boxes and invalid marketing consent
Explain the FTFC tests for unfair contract terms and switching barriers, and the training duty in paragraph 8.6

cards.title: The two-page problem
cards.setting: Products and Disclosure team, Pelangi Utama Bank Berhad, Kuala Lumpur. Tuesday, 10:15 am.

lines.text: Our new home loan app goes live next month. Marketing wants a big banner saying 'zero entry cost' right above the Product Disclosure Sheet.
Customers love that line. And honestly, nobody reads the PDS on a phone anyway.
That's exactly why BNM rewrote the disclosure rules. The new document expects the PDS to be read, not scrolled past.
Also, legal wants a pre-ticked box saying the customer agrees to share data with our insurance partner. Saves a click.
Three red flags in one launch plan. Let's walk the Fine Print Gallery and fix them before BNM does it for us.

scenes.heading: The 2024 policy document
scenes.narration: BNM issued the Product Transparency and Disclosure policy document on 2 December 2024. It replaced the 2013 guidelines and applies to licensed banks, including digital banks.

scenes.heading: What it aims for
scenes.narration: Its objectives include helping consumers understand and compare products, promoting informed decisions and minimising mis-selling.

scenes.heading: Digital first
scenes.narration: A new section on digital disclosure took effect on 1 January 2026, because small screens and one-tap purchases make it easy to skip important information.

scenes.heading: Phased dates
scenes.narration: Rules on disclosing customer information for marketing applied from 1 July 2025. The new PDS rules applied to new products from 1 July 2025 and to existing products from 1 January 2026.

scenes.heading: People, not just paper
scenes.narration: Senior management must ensure that staff and intermediaries, especially those who sell or market products, are adequately trained on the disclosure rules for those products.

cards.title: Product Transparency and Disclosure: key dates
cards.caption: Effective dates come from paragraph 4.1 of the policy document. Always check BNM's website for later amendments.

items.label: Policy document issued and in force
items.detail: General requirements apply from issuance, replacing the 2013 Guidelines on Product Transparency and Disclosure.

items.label: Marketing consent and new-product PDS
items.detail: Paragraph 12 on disclosing customer information for marketing, and the PDS rules for new products, take effect.

items.label: Digital disclosure and existing PDS
items.detail: Paragraph 11 on digital disclosure applies, and PDS rules extend to existing products.

cards.title: The five key disclosure principles
cards.caption: Paragraph 9.1 of the policy document. The principles work together; failing one usually undermines the others.

items.label: Timely
items.detail: Information arrives early enough to shape the decision, at every stage of the contract.

items.label: Clear and simple
items.detail: Plain language, readable fonts, jargon explained on the same page.

items.label: Accurate, relevant, sufficient
items.detail: Features, risks, fees and rights; risks as prominent as benefits.

items.label: Highlight what matters
items.detail: Penalties, exclusions, early termination costs and warnings stand out.

items.label: Consistent and comparable
items.detail: A standard Product Disclosure Sheet lets consumers compare offers.

cards.question: A bank shows its fixed deposit returns in large bold type and the early withdrawal penalty in grey footnote text. Which disclosure principle is most clearly breached?
options: Highlight important information, because penalties and restrictions must be given due prominence
Timely disclosure, because the penalty should only be shown after the deposit is placed
Consistent disclosure, because all banks must charge the same withdrawal penalty
cards.explanation: Paragraph 9.5.1 requires major terms such as penalties and early termination consequences to be highlighted, and paragraph 9.4.3 wants risks as prominent as benefits. Showing it later would make things worse, and banks are not required to charge the same penalty.

cards.title: Three stages of disclosure
cards.body:
Paragraph 9.2.2 requires information at **three stages** of the contract:

- **Pre-contractual**: key features, significant risks, benefits, fees and charges, and terms affecting rights and obligations, enough to compare with other banks. The PDS must be given at this stage (16.10).
- **Point of entering the contract**: rights and obligations, fees payable later, **cooling-off rights** where they apply, key exclusions, liability for loss, and contact details for enquiries and complaints (10.3.3). Customers must be advised to read the PDS and ask questions first.
- **During the term**: notice of changes **before** they take effect, regular statements without charge, and answers when the customer asks.

Two firm rules: a ticked 'I have read and understood' box can never be the bank's **sole defence** in a dispute (10.3.5), and **pre-ticked boxes** in application forms are prohibited (10.3.6).

cards.title: Which stage is it?
cards.prompt: Sort each disclosure into the stage of the contract where it belongs.

items.text: Handing over the PDS so the customer can compare offers
Explaining the effective interest rate and total repayment before applying
Pointing out cooling-off rights and their duration
Stating fees payable after acquisition and when they fall due
Giving contact details for enquiries and complaints in the contract pack
Sending notice of a fee change before it takes effect
Issuing a free periodic statement
Answering a customer's request for her outstanding balance

lines.text: Fine. What exactly is wrong with 'zero entry cost' in the banner?
BNM's prohibited business conduct guidance gives that phrase as an example of misleading conduct in property financing where the costs are passed back to the customer during the loan.
And the banner above the PDS?
For digital channels the PDS must be displayed prominently with no promotional content on the same page, and the customer can't move on until they confirm they've read it.
And the pre-ticked data-sharing box goes too, I assume.
It does. Consent to share data for marketing must be explicit and deliberate. Let's redesign the journey now.

cards.title: Telemarketing a personal loan
cards.situation: Pelangi Utama's outbound sales team calls existing customers to offer a pre-approved personal loan. Agents cannot hand over a paper PDS on a phone call, and the script currently says only 'all details are in your loan agreement'. The team leader asks you how to handle disclosure.

choices.text: Direct each customer to the PDS on the bank's website before they commit, explain the key terms and costs on the call, and record that this was done.
choices.outcome: Paragraph 16.11 allows a bank to direct consumers to its website for the PDS when providing it is impractical, such as in telemarketing. Explaining key terms and keeping evidence supports the pre-contractual duty.

choices.text: Send the PDS by post together with the signed loan agreement after approval.
choices.outcome: Too late. The PDS belongs to the pre-contractual stage so customers can compare before deciding.

choices.text: Text customers a link to the PDS so they can read it before the call ends.
choices.outcome: The intent is good, but paragraph 11.11 bars hyperlinks in SMS to reduce scam risk; tell customers how to reach the PDS instead.

cards.front: How long can a PDS be?
cards.back: No more than two A4 pages, in an easily readable font size (paragraph 16.4).
At the pre-contractual stage (16.10); for telemarketing, direct the customer to the website (16.11).

cards.front: Can it sit next to an ad?
cards.back: Not on digital channels: no promotional information on the same page as the PDS (11.7).
No. They cannot proceed until they confirm they have read the whole PDS (11.8).
Take extra steps, such as post-sale calls, to confirm the customer knows the key terms and risks (16.8).
Prioritise Bahasa Melayu, and offer forms and the PDS in languages that suit the customer base (14.1, 14.2).

cards.title: Valid and invalid marketing consent
cards.caption: Paragraph 12.2 of the PTD policy document. After withdrawal, a reasonable time to stop sharing is not more than seven calendar days.

items.label: Specific
items.left: 'We may share your data with partners'
items.right: Names who receives it, why, and what data

items.label: Voluntary
items.left: Consent is a condition of the loan
items.right: Loan is available whether or not she agrees

items.label: Revocable
items.right: Withdrawal as easy as giving consent

cards.question: A customer withdraws consent for her data to be shared with the bank's insurance partner for marketing. What does the PTD policy document treat as a reasonable time to stop the sharing?
options: At the next annual review of her account
Only once her current loan has been fully repaid
Not more than seven calendar days from receiving the withdrawal
cards.explanation: Paragraph 12.2(d) says the bank must stop as soon as practicable, and a reasonable time frame is not more than seven calendar days from receiving the notice.

cards.title: Fair terms under FTFC
cards.body:
Disclosure cannot rescue an unfair contract. FTFC paragraph 11 adds:

- **Unfair terms**: a standard-contract term is unfair if it tends to create a **significant imbalance**, shifting rights and obligations significantly in the bank's favour to the consumer's detriment (11.4). Appendix 4 lists terms BNM is likely to see as unfair.
- **Plain, legible, prominent**: terms are reviewed during product development; obligations on the consumer get appropriate prominence (11.6).
- **No switching barriers**: consumers must be able to switch product or provider without **disproportionate costs** (11.7).
- **Key terms in the PDS** for every product (11.9), plus a clear reminder to read the terms and ask about anything unclear (11.8).
- **Old contracts too**: a bank must not enforce or invoke unfair terms in contracts that existed before the document (11.11).

cards.title: Grace's home loan redesign
cards.body:
After the review, Grace's team changed the home loan journey:

- The 'zero entry cost' banner was removed; legal fees and who pays them now appear in the PDS fee section.
- The PDS screen carries no promotions, has a 'reading time' cue and a download button, and the 'Next' button stays inactive until the customer confirms reading it.
- The data-sharing box is unticked, standalone and names the partner, the purpose and the data.
- An early settlement charge that ran for the whole tenure was cut back after Nurul Aina asked whether it created a switching barrier.
- Sales staff and mortgage agents completed a short module on the new disclosure rules before launch, as paragraph 8.6 expects.

Result: the launch slipped by a week, but the product passed the conduct sign-off on the first attempt.

cards.title: Stage 2 takeaways
items: The PTD policy document (2 December 2024) phases in: marketing consent and new-product PDS from 1 July 2025, digital disclosure and existing products from 1 January 2026.
Five principles: timely; clear and simple; accurate, relevant and sufficient; highlight important information; consistent and comparable.
Disclose at three stages; a PDS of no more than two A4 pages goes out before the contract, and no pre-ticked boxes.
Marketing consent must be specific, voluntary, explicit and revocable.
Unfair terms and switching barriers break FTFC even when they are disclosed, and sellers must be trained on disclosure rules.

cards.prompt: Pick a document or screen you give customers. Would a first-time customer, reading in Bahasa Melayu on a phone, find the key fee and risk within ten seconds? What one change would make that happen?

quiz.question: Under the Product Transparency and Disclosure policy document, what is the maximum length of a Product Disclosure Sheet?
options: Four A4 pages
There is no length limit
Two A4 pages
One A4 page
quiz.explanation: Paragraph 16.4 says the PDS must not exceed two A4 pages and must use an easily readable font size.

quiz.question: A customer applies online for a credit card. The application form has a box, already ticked, adding a card protection plan. What does the PTD policy document say?
options: Pre-ticked boxes in a product application form are prohibited
They are allowed for digital channels but not for branch forms
They are allowed if the plan can be cancelled within a year
They are allowed if the add-on appears in the monthly statement
quiz.explanation: Paragraph 10.3.6 prohibits pre-ticked boxes because they co-opt consumers into buying products without explicit consent. Cancellation rights or later disclosure do not cure it.

quiz.question: A dispute arises and the bank's only evidence is that the customer ticked 'I have read and understood the PDS'. Why is this weak?
options: The bank may not rely on that acknowledgement as its sole defence
The PDS must be signed in ink to have any legal effect
Acknowledgements expire after the cooling-off period ends
A tick box is valid only if a witness was present at the time
quiz.explanation: Paragraph 10.3.5 says a tick or signature on the PDS must not be the bank's sole defence in a dispute about the disclosed terms. Banks need evidence that they actually explained the key terms.

quiz.question: Your bank wants to tell customers about an important change to card fees on its app. Which approach fits paragraph 11.11 of the PTD policy document?
options: Send an SMS containing a short link that opens the fee page
Post the change on the website only and wait for questions
Email a link asking customers to log in with their password
Send an SMS or push notice explaining how to view the change, without a hyperlink in the SMS
quiz.explanation: Paragraph 11.11 requires timely notice through instant channels with details on how to access the disclosure, but bans hyperlinks in SMS to reduce scam risk. Website-only notice is not timely.

quiz.question: Which item must be disclosed at the point of entering into a contract under paragraph 10.3.3?
options: Cooling-off rights and their duration, where applicable
The bank's internal credit scoring model
The salesperson's monthly sales target
The names of other customers on the same product
quiz.explanation: Paragraph 10.3.3 lists rights and obligations, later fees, cooling-off rights, key exclusions, liability for loss and contact details. Sales targets and scoring models are internal, and other customers' names are secret.

quiz.question: An investment-linked product aims to return the customer's capital but has no explicit guarantee. Marketing wants to call it 'capital guaranteed'. What is the rule?
options: It may be called capital guaranteed for customers over 60 only
It may not be presented as capital guaranteed without an explicit guarantee from a licensed FSP
It may be called capital guaranteed if a risk warning appears in the footnotes
It may be called capital guaranteed if past returns were always positive
quiz.explanation: Paragraph 9.4.6 bars representing a product that merely aims to return capital as capital guaranteed unless the guarantee is explicitly provided by the bank or another BNM-licensed FSP.

quiz.question: Which group must senior management ensure is adequately trained on the disclosure requirements, according to paragraph 8.6?
options: Only external auditors, because they test disclosure
Staff and intermediaries, particularly those who sell or market financial products
Only the Board, because it approves disclosure policies
Only IT developers, because they build the digital channels
quiz.explanation: Paragraph 8.6 focuses on staff and intermediaries involved in selling or marketing. The Board oversees, auditors review and developers build, but the explicit training duty points at sellers and marketers.

quiz.question: A home loan contract lets the bank change any fee at any time without notice, while the borrower must pay a heavy penalty to switch banks in year eight. Under FTFC, what is the main concern?
options: The terms may be unfair and create a switching barrier with disproportionate costs
The only problem is that the contract is not in English
The terms are fine because the borrower signed the contract
The terms are fine provided they appear in the PDS
quiz.explanation: Paragraph 11.4 treats terms causing a significant imbalance as unfair, and 11.7 bars barriers that make switching costly. Disclosure or a signature does not make an unfair term fair.

quiz.question: A customer asks to sign the Bahasa Melayu version of her personal loan agreement instead of the English one. What must the bank do?
options: Allow it only after she pays a translation fee
Allow her to sign the Bahasa Melayu version
Ask her to sign both versions in front of a lawyer
Refuse, because contracts may only be in one language
quiz.explanation: Paragraph 14.5 says that if a consumer asks for the Bahasa Melayu version of a form, contract or agreement, the bank must let her sign it. Paragraph 14.1 also asks banks to prioritise Bahasa Melayu.

quiz.question: An advertisement for a savings account says 'FREE gift for every new account', but the gift requires a minimum balance for 12 months. What does the PTD policy document require?
options: Do not call the gift free if conditions apply, and give enough information about them
Keep 'free' but add the conditions on the bank's website only
Remove the gift, because gifts are banned in bank advertising
Keep 'free' because the gift itself costs the customer nothing
quiz.explanation: Paragraph 13.2.7 bars describing a promotional gift as free where conditions are attached, and requires sufficient information about any conditions. Gifts are not banned outright.

sessions.title: Fair Dealing, Suitable Advice and Prohibited Business Conduct
sessions.summary: How Malaysian bank staff must sell and advise: FTFC fair dealing and suitability, commission disclosure and competence checks, the six practices banned by FSA section 124 and Schedule 7, BNM's Prohibited Business Conduct guidance, and lending responsibly.
objectives: List the six prohibited business conduct practices in Schedule 7 of the FSA and apply BNM's examples
Carry out a suitability assessment using the factors in FTFC paragraph 14.8
Explain the duties to disclose commission, avoid undue pressure and keep advisers competent
Describe in general terms what responsible lending means, including affordability and avoiding predatory sales

cards.title: The pensioner and the brochure
cards.setting: Pelangi Utama branch, Ipoh. Wednesday, 3:40 pm.

lines.text: Arif has a brochure open on his desk when Encik Rahim, 67, sits down with his retirement savings book.
Pak cik, this investment-linked plan pays much better than your fixed deposit. The campaign closes Friday, so we should sign today.
Arif, a word? Daniel, branch manager. Does the campaign really close Friday?
Well, there's always another campaign next month.
Then saying it closes Friday is a false deadline. And have you checked whether Encik Rahim can afford to lose part of that capital?
Good catch, Daniel. That conversation touched three different rules in two minutes. Welcome to the Sales Floor.

scenes.heading: The hard floor: Schedule 7
scenes.narration: Section 124 of the Financial Services Act says a bank must not engage in the prohibited business conduct listed in Schedule 7. Breaching it is a criminal offence under the Act.

scenes.heading: BNM's guidance
scenes.narration: BNM's Prohibited Business Conduct policy document, issued in July 2016, explains what each banned practice looks like and the factors BNM weighs. Banks answer for their agents and outsourced providers too.

scenes.heading: The higher standard: FTFC
scenes.narration: The fair treatment policy document adds positive duties: due care, skill and diligence, no undue pressure, suitable advice and disclosure of commission.

scenes.heading: Responsible lending
scenes.narration: The Act lets BNM set standards on assessing suitability and affordability, so lending decisions must check that the customer can meet the repayments.

cards.title: The six prohibited practices in Schedule 7
cards.caption: Schedule 7 of the FSA 2013. Complaints about items 5 and 6 are referred by BNM to the Competition Commission under section 124(5).

items.label: 1. Misleading or deceptive conduct
items.detail: About the nature, features, terms or price of a product.

items.label: 2. Inducing by false or reckless statements
items.detail: Misleading promises, forecasts or comparisons, or dishonestly hiding material facts.

items.label: 3. Undue pressure or harassment
items.detail: Pressure, coercion, harassment or force when selling or collecting payment.

items.label: 4. Demanding payment for unsolicited products
items.detail: Charging for products the consumer never accepted.

items.label: 5. Coercive bundling
items.detail: Forcing a consumer to buy one product as a condition of getting another.

items.label: 6. Collusion
items.detail: Fixing product features or terms with others to consumers' detriment.

cards.title: Prohibited or permitted?
cards.prompt: Using BNM's Prohibited Business Conduct guidance, sort each practice.

items.text: Telling a customer an offer ends Friday when it does not
Calling a non-principal-protected product a deposit
Requiring credit shield cover before approving a new credit card
Calling a customer repeatedly after she said she is not interested
Charging a customer for an add-on she never agreed to
Requiring fire insurance on a property used for home financing
Offering a cheaper bundle while still selling each product separately
Telling a borrower in arrears the lawful consequences of not paying

cards.question: A banker tells a grieving widow, two days after her husband's funeral, that she must buy a savings-linked insurance plan today. Which prohibited practice is this most likely to be?
options: Exerting undue pressure or influence by exploiting her emotional state
Collusion with another bank to fix the plan's terms
Demanding payment for an unsolicited financial service
cards.explanation: BNM's guidance gives exploiting a consumer's obvious emotional state, such as grief, as an example of undue pressure under paragraph 3 of Schedule 7. There is no collusion or unsolicited billing here.

cards.title: Suitable advice under FTFC
cards.body:
When staff advise or recommend, FTFC paragraph 14 applies:

- Advice needs a **reasonable basis** and must be in the consumer's **best interests** (14.3).
- Assess whether the product suits the consumer's **objectives, needs, circumstances, financial situation, risk appetite and investment horizon**; whether they have the **knowledge and experience** to understand it; whether they can **meet the commitments**; and whether the risk fits their **risk tolerance** (14.8).
- Tell consumers that inaccurate information affects the advice (14.7), and show them **all products assessed as suitable** (14.9).
- If capital could be lost, make sure they understand that risk **before** advising (14.10).
- **Disclose commission** before advising, as a percentage of what the consumer pays (14.12, 14.13), and never recommend a product just to earn more (14.14).
- The bank must be able to **demonstrate** suitability (14.11).

cards.title: A suitability conversation
cards.prompt: Arrange the steps of a fair advice conversation in order.
steps: Disclose any commission the bank will receive, as a percentage
Gather the customer's objectives, circumstances, finances, risk appetite and horizon
Explain that inaccurate information will affect the suitability of advice
Assess knowledge, ability to meet commitments and risk tolerance
Present all products assessed as suitable, with key terms and risks
Give time to read the product information and consider the advice
Record the basis for the recommendation so suitability can be demonstrated

lines.text: Okay. I dropped the Friday deadline. Encik Rahim says his savings are for his medical costs and he's never invested before.
So his horizon is short, his knowledge is limited and his capacity for loss is low. What does that tell you?
That the plan probably isn't suitable. But it's the campaign product.
FTFC even lists this as a predatory example: pushing retirees into higher-risk investment-linked or unit trust products for higher returns without explaining the downside.
Show him the options that do fit, write up why, and let him go home and think. That's how we keep his trust.

cards.title: The credit card at the university fair
cards.situation: Pelangi Utama has a booth at a university open day. A regional manager suggests signing up students for credit cards with a free power bank for every approved application. Arif is asked to staff the booth and wonders whether this is acceptable.

choices.text: Raise it with Consumer Conduct: FTFC lists promoting credit cards to university students as a predatory example, so the plan should be stopped or redesigned around suitable products.
choices.outcome: Paragraph 16.10 gives promoting credit cards to university students as an example of predatory practice. Escalating before the event is the right move.

choices.text: Staff the booth but only approve students who say they have a part-time job.
choices.outcome: This reduces some risk but still runs a campaign that BNM lists as predatory, and self-declared income is weak evidence of affordability.

choices.text: Go ahead, since students are adults and can decide for themselves.
choices.outcome: Consumers' own choices matter, but the bank must not use sales practices that exploit vulnerable groups or lead to unaffordable debt.

cards.title: Need versus capacity: reading a lending request
cards.caption: An aid for discussion, not a BNM formula. FTFC 14.8(c) asks whether the consumer can meet the commitments, and 16.10 warns against enticing highly indebted consumers into new unsecured loans.

items.label: Clear need, can afford
items.detail: Proceed with clear disclosure and suitable terms.

items.label: Clear need, cannot afford
items.detail: Do not push; explore smaller amounts, longer terms or other help.

items.label: Weak need, can afford
items.detail: Explain options; never upsell to hit targets.

items.label: Weak need, cannot afford
items.detail: Highest harm; predatory if the bank entices it.

cards.front: What does the FSA allow BNM to require?
cards.back: Standards on advice, including assessing the suitability and affordability of products offered to consumers (section 123(2)(d)).
Whether the consumer is likely to meet the financial commitments of the product (FTFC 14.8(c)).
Those already highly indebted with low savings; enticing them into new unsecured loans is a predatory example.
In BNM's lending and responsible financing standards; check the current versions on BNM's website.
It can assist, but banks must take due care with AI and machine learning in credit assessment to avoid unfair discrimination (FTFC 16.12).

cards.question: Before recommending a unit trust, what must Arif disclose about commission under FTFC?
options: Nothing, unless the customer specifically asks how he is paid
Only the total commission the branch earned in the last quarter
The amount of commission, as a percentage of what the consumer pays, before giving the advice
cards.explanation: Paragraphs 14.12 and 14.13 require the quantum of commission to be disclosed as a percentage before any advice or recommendation is given.

cards.title: Keeping advisers competent
Stage 3 takeaways
items: FSA section 124 bans the six Schedule 7 practices: misleading, inducing by false statements, undue pressure, billing unsolicited products, coercive bundling and collusion.
BNM's 2016 guidance gives concrete examples, such as false deadlines, 'zero entry cost' claims and credit shield as a condition for a card.
Suitable advice rests on the customer's needs, knowledge, capacity to pay and risk tolerance, and must be demonstrable.
Disclose commission as a percentage before advising, and never recommend for higher gain alone.
Lend responsibly: check affordability and never entice vulnerable or over-indebted customers into unsuitable credit.

cards.prompt: Recall a sale or recommendation you made recently. Could you show a supervisor, from the file alone, why it suited that customer and that you disclosed what you had to?

quiz.question: Under the Financial Services Act 2013, where is the list of prohibited business conduct for banks found?
options: Section 126 on the ombudsman scheme
Schedule 7, given force by section 124
Section 133 on secrecy
Schedule 11, given force by section 134
quiz.explanation: Section 124(1) bars financial service providers from the conduct listed in Schedule 7. Schedule 11 lists permitted disclosures of customer information, and section 126 deals with the ombudsman scheme.

quiz.question: A bank requires every applicant for a new personal financing facility to buy an insurance policy from its partner, with no option to decline. What does BNM's guidance say?
options: It is allowed if the premium is disclosed in the PDS
It is an example of coercing consumers to buy one product as a condition for another
It is a collusion issue only for the Competition Commission
It is allowed because insurance always protects the borrower
quiz.explanation: BNM's Prohibited Business Conduct guidance lists requiring insurance as a condition for a new personal financing facility as coercion under paragraph 5 of Schedule 7. Disclosure does not cure coercion.

quiz.question: Which bundling arrangement does BNM's guidance treat as permissible?
options: Requiring credit shield cover to approve a new credit card
Requiring personal accident cover to get motor insurance
Pricing single products so high that only the bundle is realistic
Requiring fire insurance for a property under home financing
quiz.explanation: The guidance expressly allows requiring fire insurance or mortgage reducing term assurance for home financing. The other three appear as examples of direct or indirect coercion.

quiz.question: A debt collection agent acting for your bank tells a borrower that he will be jailed tomorrow unless he pays. What is the main problem?
options: Only that the threat should have been approved by the branch manager
Threatening action that cannot legally be taken is undue pressure, and the bank answers for its agents
Only that the agent should have written instead of calling
Nothing, because the bank is entitled to collect debts in any way
quiz.explanation: BNM's guidance allows debt collection and advice on lawful consequences but not threats of legally impossible action. Banks are responsible for agents and service providers complying with the prohibitions.

quiz.question: Which set of factors must staff assess for suitability under FTFC paragraph 14.8?
options: Needs and circumstances, knowledge and experience, ability to meet commitments and risk tolerance
The product's profit margin and the branch's monthly target
Age, gender, religion and marital status of the customer
Only the customer's income as shown on the latest payslip
quiz.explanation: Paragraph 14.8 lists needs and circumstances, knowledge and experience, ability to meet commitments and risk-reward fit. Arbitrary factors like religion or marital status must not drive less favourable treatment under 13.8.

quiz.question: A retiree with no investment experience asks for somewhere safe for her savings. A banker suggests a complex investment-linked product, stressing higher returns. Under FTFC, how is this best described?
options: Acceptable if the product has performed well in the past
A predatory practice of the kind paragraph 16.10 gives as an example
Acceptable if she signs a waiver of the bank's liability
Good advice, because higher returns are in every customer's interest
quiz.explanation: Paragraph 16.10 lists promoting complex investment-linked products to consumers with no investment experience, and misleading retirees about higher returns, as predatory. Waivers excluding liability are a listed poor practice.

quiz.question: Which statement about commission disclosure under FTFC is correct?
options: It is confidential and may never be shared with customers
It must be disclosed in ringgit after the contract is signed
It need only be disclosed if the customer is a business
The amount must be disclosed as a percentage before advice is given
quiz.explanation: Paragraphs 14.12 and 14.13 require disclosure of the quantum of commission, expressed as a percentage of the amount paid, before providing advice or a recommendation.

quiz.question: Which measure does FTFC paragraph 13.3 require so that staff do not mislead consumers about products?
options: Rotation of sales staff between branches every six months
A ban on staff discussing product risks with customers
A signed undertaking from each customer not to rely on staff statements
Training, supervision and monitoring of staff, representatives and agents
quiz.explanation: Paragraph 13.3 requires training, supervision and monitoring. Making customers waive reliance on staff would breach 13.4, which bars excluding liability for staff misleading consumers.

quiz.question: Under section 124 of the Financial Services Act, what happens to complaints about coercive bundling or collusion (paragraphs 5 and 6 of Schedule 7)?
options: The bank must refer them to the police
BNM refers them to the Competition Commission
They go directly to the ombudsman scheme
BNM refers them to the Securities Commission
quiz.explanation: Section 124(5) requires BNM to refer complaints involving paragraphs 5 and 6 of Schedule 7 to the Competition Commission, which BNM also consults when issuing guidance on them.

quiz.question: How must a bank check that its advisers stay competent over time under FTFC paragraph 14.16?
options: By relying on the adviser's own declaration each year
By counting the number of products each adviser has sold
Through a periodic process, which can include customer feedback on how products were explained
Through a one-off test at recruitment that never needs repeating
quiz.explanation: Paragraph 14.16 requires a process to periodically check competence and gives obtaining consumer feedback as an example. A one-off test, self-declaration or sales count does not test the quality of advice.

sessions.title: Vulnerable Consumers, Complaints Handling and the Ombudsman
sessions.summary: FTFC Principle 7 on vulnerable consumers (from 1 April 2025), BNM's Complaints Handling policy document (in force from 1 April 2026) with its turnaround times and training duty, and the routes onward to the Financial Markets Ombudsman Service and BNMLINK.
objectives: Recognise the four categories of vulnerable consumer and respond within FTFC paragraphs 16.15 to 16.17
Apply the Complaints Handling turnaround times for acknowledgement, simple, complex and exceptional cases
Write a final decision that meets paragraph 12.2 and refer the customer correctly to FMOS or BNMLINK
Explain the training duty for complaints staff in paragraph 9.4

cards.title: The call that went wrong
cards.setting: Complaints Handling Unit, Pelangi Utama Bank Berhad, Petaling Jaya. Thursday, 9:05 am.

lines.text: Morning. Listen to this one. Puan Lee, 72, phoned three times about a card charge. Each time she had to explain from scratch that she has poor eyesight and can't read our SMS.
On the third call an agent told her to 'just check the app'. She cried. Her son has now posted about it on social media.
Is a social media post even a complaint? Nobody filled in a form.
Under BNM's Complaints Handling policy document, a complaint is any expression of dissatisfaction, through any channel, including social media. And Puan Lee is a vulnerable consumer.
So we failed twice: once on vulnerability, once on complaints. Help me fix both before BNM asks.

cards.title: Who counts as a vulnerable consumer?

scenes.heading: Access challenges
scenes.narration: People who may struggle to access financial services or need help to use them, such as persons with disabilities or senior citizens, meaning people aged 60 and above.

scenes.heading: Low resilience
scenes.narration: People with little ability to absorb a financial shock, such as those who are over-indebted or have no savings.

scenes.heading: Adverse life events
scenes.narration: People facing hardship after events such as natural disasters, loss of income, unemployment, or the death or total disability of the main breadwinner.

scenes.heading: Literacy and language
scenes.narration: People with low financial literacy or experience, poor language skills, illiteracy, or who are not digitally savvy, for example speaking neither Bahasa Malaysia nor English.

scenes.heading: It can change
scenes.narration: Vulnerability is not a fixed label. Anyone can become vulnerable at some stage of life or of the product life cycle, so staff need to notice the signs.

cards.title: Recognise, assess, respond
cards.caption: FTFC paragraph 16.15 requires training to recognise, assess and respond to vulnerable consumers' needs; 16.17 covers escalation and 16.19 covers recording.

items.label: Recognise
items.detail: Notice signs and indicators of vulnerability; encourage disclosure where indicators are clear.

items.label: Assess
items.detail: Understand the customer's needs and whether they are temporary or long-term.

items.label: Respond
items.detail: Adapt channel, pace and solution; use the flexibility the bank gives you.

items.label: Escalate
items.detail: Know when to bring in a supervisor or a specialist team.

items.label: Record
items.detail: Capture needs so colleagues can help without the customer repeating the story.

cards.title: Which vulnerability category?
cards.prompt: Sort each customer into the FTFC category that fits best.

items.text: A 68-year-old who struggles with the banking app's small text
A wheelchair user who cannot reach the branch counter
A customer with several unpaid credit cards and no savings
A trader whose shop was destroyed in a flood
A widow whose husband was the household's only earner
A customer who speaks only Tamil and cannot read the English PDS
A first-time user who has never had a bank account

cards.question: A customer mentions she has a disability that is not visible. What does FTFC say about verifying this?
options: The bank may offer voluntary ways to confirm it, but must not compel or use them against her
The bank must demand a medical report before giving any extra help
The bank should ignore disabilities that are not visible
cards.explanation: A footnote to the FTFC definition lists voluntary options, such as a medical letter or an OKU card, and says such procedures should not be compelled on or used against the consumer.

cards.title: The Complaints Handling policy document
cards.body:
BNM issued a new **Complaints Handling** policy document on **28 March 2025**. It replaced the 2009 guidelines and applies from **1 April 2026**, except the referral rules in paragraphs 12.1 to 12.4, which applied immediately.

Key building blocks:
- **Wide definition**: any expression of dissatisfaction, **justified or not**, in person or in writing, through any channel including call centres, websites and social media. Grievances from the bank's own employees or agents are excluded.
- **Board and senior management** own the governance framework, resources, channels and escalation (paragraph 7).
- **Centralised complaints platform** that collects complaints from every channel (9.2).
- **Dedicated complaints function** acting independently and impartially (9.3).
- **Easy access**: a 'Contact Us' tab at the top of the homepage, one click to the complaints page (10.3).
- **Independent periodic reviews** of the function, for example by compliance or internal audit (11.14).

cards.title: Complaint turnaround times
cards.caption: Days count from receipt of the complaint. Complaints about unauthorised e-banking transactions follow BNM's separate requirements instead (11.2).

items.label: Written acknowledgement
items.detail: Includes a contact point and the estimated turnaround time (11.3).

items.label: Simple case decided
items.detail: Or tell the customer the case is complex, with the new timeline and reasons (11.5, 11.7).

items.label: Complex case decided
items.detail: With progress updates at least every 10 working days (11.6, 11.12).

items.label: Third-party information
items.detail: 10 extra days if reports such as medical, forensic or police are needed; chase every 5 days (11.8, 11.11).

items.label: Exceptional circumstances
items.detail: Senior management makes a final decision without the missing document (11.9).

cards.title: Match the deadline
cards.prompt: Link each requirement of the Complaints Handling policy document to its time limit.

pairs.right: By the next working day after receiving the complaint
No later than 5 working days from receipt
No later than 20 working days from receipt

pairs.left: Progress updates on a complex case
pairs.right: At least once every 10 working days
Within 10 working days of receiving them
At least once every 5 working days

cards.title: Fixing Puan Lee's case
cards.setting: Complaints Handling Unit, later that morning.

lines.text: Logged on the central platform as a complaint received via social media yesterday. Acknowledgement goes out today, by letter in large print, since SMS doesn't work for her.
The charge investigation needs the card scheme's records. That makes it complex: 20 working days, unless we need third-party documents.
Then tell her within five working days that it's complex, why, and the new timeline. And record her eyesight need so no one asks her again.
What if we decide against her in the end?
Written decision, plain language, reasons, and how to take it to the ombudsman if she's still unhappy. Treating her fairly doesn't mean she always wins.

cards.title: The final decision letter
cards.situation: Kavitha's team has finished investigating a complaint about a late-payment charge. The charge was correctly applied under the card terms. The customer, who reads Bahasa Malaysia better than English, is likely to be unhappy. A junior officer drafts a two-line English email: 'Your complaint is rejected under clause 14.3. This matter is closed.'

choices.text: Rewrite it in plain language with the reasons, highlight anything that affects her, offer a Bahasa Malaysia translation, and explain how to go to FMOS or BNMLINK.
choices.outcome: This meets paragraph 12.2: plain-language reasons, prominence for material information, translation where language is a barrier, and accurate information on redress avenues.

choices.text: Send it as drafted, since the bank's decision is correct.
choices.outcome: A correct decision still needs a compliant explanation. A clause number with no reasons and no redress information falls short of paragraph 12.2.

choices.text: Add a sentence of apology and send it in English.
choices.outcome: Courtesy helps, but the letter still lacks reasons, translation and the routes to FMOS or BNMLINK.

cards.back: The Financial Markets Ombudsman Service, launched in January 2025 by merging the Ombudsman for Financial Services and SIDREC.

cards.front: When must a bank refer a customer to FMOS?
cards.back: When the customer is an eligible complainant and the dispute is within FMOS's jurisdiction, or when both sides agree to refer it (12.3).

cards.front: What if FMOS has no jurisdiction?
cards.back: If the bank or customer does not agree to an FMOS referral, the bank refers the customer to BNMLINK (12.4).
BNM said on its launch that eligible disputes can be awarded up to RM250,000.

cards.front: Must banks join an ombudsman scheme?
cards.back: FSA section 126 lets regulations require it, and members must provide documents and comply with awards.
Yes. Paragraph 15.10 requires banks to tell consumers about alternative dispute resolution if they want to pursue a closed case.

cards.title: Complaints in numbers (BNM, January 2025)
cards.caption: Figures from the Deputy Governor's speech at the launch of FMOS, 17 January 2025, published on bnm.gov.my.

items.label: Complaints in five years
items.detail: Received by the financial industry over the five years before FMOS's launch.

items.label: From the banking sector
items.detail: The rest came from insurance and takaful.

items.label: Fall in BNMLINK complaints
items.detail: Over the same period, as banks' own complaint channels improved.

items.label: FMOS award limit
items.detail: Streamlined maximum for eligible disputes at FMOS's launch.

cards.question: Paragraph 9.4 of the Complaints Handling policy document sets requirements for staff in the complaints function. Which is one of them?
options: They must hold a law degree before handling complex cases
They must receive adequate and continuous training, including on engaging with vulnerable consumers
They must report to the sales director so that complaints are linked to revenue
cards.explanation: Paragraph 9.4 requires complaints staff to be empowered to resolve complaints and to receive adequate and continuous training to assess complaints fairly and engage professionally with diverse and vulnerable consumers. Independence from sales matters too.

cards.title: Five habits for the Listening Desk
cards.body:
- **Log everything**, whatever the channel: a tweet, a branch remark or an email are all complaints.
- **Name the clock** in your acknowledgement: who is handling it and the estimated turnaround time.
- **Record vulnerability needs** once, so the customer never has to repeat them.
- **Explain, don't cite**: reasons in plain language, terms explained, translation where needed.
- **Always end with the way forward**: FMOS if eligible, or BNMLINK.

cards.title: Stage 4 takeaways
items: Vulnerable consumers fall into four broad categories, and anyone can become vulnerable; training must help staff recognise, assess, respond and escalate.
From 1 April 2026, any expression of dissatisfaction through any channel is a complaint and goes to a central platform.
Acknowledge by the next working day; decide simple cases in 5 and complex cases in 20 working days, with defined extensions.
Final decisions are written, reasoned, in plain language, translated where needed, and point to FMOS or BNMLINK.
Complaints staff must be empowered and receive adequate, continuous training (paragraph 9.4).

cards.prompt: Think of the last unhappy customer you dealt with. Did their dissatisfaction reach the central complaints platform? If not, what would you do differently next time?

quiz.question: A customer writes on the bank's Facebook page that a fee was unfairly charged, but never contacts the bank directly. Under the Complaints Handling policy document, how should this be treated?
options: As a matter for the marketing team, since it concerns social media
As public feedback only, because complaints must be made in writing to a branch
As a complaint only if the customer later fills in the official form
As a complaint, because it expresses dissatisfaction through one of the bank's channels
quiz.explanation: The definition covers any expression of dissatisfaction, justified or not, made through any channel; a footnote names social media. It must reach the centralised complaints platform.

quiz.question: By when must a bank send written acknowledgement of a complaint?
options: Within 5 working days
Only once the case is resolved
Within 10 calendar days
Within the next working day of receiving it
quiz.explanation: Paragraph 11.3 requires written acknowledgement within the next working day, including a contact point and the estimated turnaround time.

quiz.question: A complaint is logged as simple on day 1. On day 4 the officer realises it needs input from three departments. What must the bank do?
options: Notify the customer within 5 working days of receipt that it is complex, with the new timeline and reasons
Keep it as simple and accept that the deadline will be missed
Wait until the 20th working day before telling the customer anything
Close the complaint and ask the customer to submit a new one
quiz.explanation: Paragraph 11.7 requires notice within 5 working days of receipt when a simple case becomes complex, stating the applicable timeline and the reasons for the extra time.

quiz.question: A complex complaint needs a police report that has not arrived by day 30. What does the policy document require?
options: Keep chasing every 5 working days, and senior management decides by day 60 at the latest
Refer the case straight to BNMLINK and stop investigating
Reject the complaint automatically because evidence is missing
Suspend the complaint indefinitely until the report arrives
quiz.explanation: Paragraphs 11.9 and 11.11 require follow-up with the third party at least every 5 working days and a senior management decision, or other measures, no later than 60 working days from receipt.

quiz.question: Which of these is NOT one of the FTFC categories of vulnerable consumer?
options: A customer who lost his job and has no savings
A customer who speaks neither Bahasa Malaysia nor English
A customer who holds a high-value private banking portfolio
A senior citizen who needs help to use digital banking
quiz.explanation: The FTFC categories are access challenges, low resilience, adverse life events, and low literacy, experience or language skills. Wealth alone does not make someone vulnerable, though any customer can become vulnerable.

quiz.question: What does FTFC paragraph 16.15 require for staff, representatives and agents?
options: Training to recognise, assess and respond appropriately to vulnerable consumers' needs
Referral of every vulnerable customer to the ombudsman scheme
A medical qualification before serving customers with disabilities
Refusal of credit to anyone who is aged 60 or above
quiz.explanation: Paragraph 16.15 requires the necessary training, especially for those with direct contact. Refusing credit because of age or referring every vulnerable customer to FMOS would itself be unfair.

quiz.question: Puan Lee had to explain her poor eyesight on each of three calls. Which FTFC requirement did the bank miss?
options: Recording vulnerable consumers' needs so other staff can access and act on them
Reviewing contract terms during product development
Disclosing commission as a percentage before giving advice
Publishing the Treat Customers Fairly Charter on its website
quiz.explanation: Paragraph 16.19 requires relevant information about vulnerable consumers' needs to be properly recorded and accessible to staff who need it; the policy lists making customers repeat sensitive information as a poor practice.

quiz.question: A complaint falls outside FMOS's jurisdiction, and the bank does not agree to refer it there. Where must the bank direct the customer?
options: The Securities Commission's investor complaints unit
Nowhere, because the bank's decision is then final
BNMLINK, Bank Negara Malaysia's information and advisory channel
The Malaysian civil courts as the only option
quiz.explanation: Paragraph 12.4 requires referral to BNMLINK where the complaint is outside FMOS's jurisdiction and either party disagrees to an FMOS referral.

quiz.question: Which of these must a final decision letter contain under paragraph 12.2 of the Complaints Handling policy document?
options: The names of the staff who were disciplined over the complaint
A copy of the bank's internal audit report on complaints
A clause stating that the customer waives any further claim
Plain-language reasons and accurate information on redress avenues
quiz.explanation: Paragraph 12.2 requires clear reasons in plain language, prominence for material information, translation where language is a barrier and information on redress. Waivers of further claims would undermine redress.

quiz.question: Which body did FMOS replace when it was launched in January 2025, according to BNM?
options: The Malaysia Competition Commission's consumer unit
The Credit Counselling and Debt Management Agency
BNMLINK, which was closed at the same time
The Ombudsman for Financial Services, merged with SIDREC
quiz.explanation: BNM's speech at the FMOS launch describes it as the result of merging the Ombudsman for Financial Services and the Securities Industry Dispute Resolution Center. BNMLINK continues to operate.

sessions.title: Customer Secrecy, Accountability and Exam Readiness
sessions.summary: Banking secrecy under FSA sections 133 and 134, BNM's 2025 Management of Customer Information and Permitted Disclosures policy document, breach escalation, a real BNM enforcement case, and a recap of every training and accountability duty in this quest before the final exam.
objectives: Explain the secrecy duty in FSA section 133, its exceptions and the permitted disclosures route in section 134
Apply the MCIPD 2025 staff awareness, training, breach escalation and outsourcing requirements
Describe what BNM's 2019 enforcement action against CIMB Bank Berhad teaches about customer information
Map the training duties across FTFC, PTD, Complaints Handling and MCIPD to roles in your bank

cards.title: The phone call from 'the police'
cards.setting: Branch operations desk, Pelangi Utama Bank Berhad, Johor Bahru. Friday, 11:20 am.

lines.text: I've been covering Johor Bahru this week. A caller says he's a police inspector and needs a customer's last six months of statements faxed today.
He sounded very official. He even gave a report number. Should we just send it? It's the police.
Stop there. Customer information is protected by the Financial Services Act. Disclosure to law enforcement is permitted, but only on BNM's conditions.
And if he isn't really police, we've just handed a fraudster everything.
Final stage. Today we cover secrecy, permitted disclosures, breaches, and then you'll be ready for the regulator's questions.

scenes.heading: Section 133: the duty
scenes.narration: Anyone with access to information about a bank customer's affairs or account, including the bank and its directors, officers and agents, must not disclose it to another person.

scenes.heading: Three narrow exceptions
scenes.narration: The ban does not cover disclosures to BNM for its functions, summaries that cannot identify any customer, or information already lawfully public from another source.

scenes.heading: Section 134: permitted disclosures
scenes.narration: A bank may also disclose for the purposes and to the persons listed in Schedule 11 of the Act, or with BNM's written approval, always subject to BNM's conditions.

scenes.heading: No passing it on
scenes.narration: A person who receives information under a permitted disclosure, or knows it was leaked, must not disclose it further. Breaches are criminal offences.

scenes.heading: The MCIPD policy document
scenes.narration: BNM's Management of Customer Information and Permitted Disclosures policy document, reissued on 31 October 2025, sets how banks protect customer information and the conditions for each permitted disclosure.

cards.title: Can I disclose this customer information?
cards.caption: Each gate narrows what can be released. If any answer is unclear, do not disclose; escalate.

items.label: Is it customer information?
items.detail: Anything about a customer's affairs or account: the default is no disclosure.

items.label: Is it a section 133 exception?
items.detail: To BNM, non-identifying summaries, or already lawfully public elsewhere.

items.label: Is it a Schedule 11 purpose?
items.detail: For example, an enforcement agency's written, specific request, or the customer's written consent.

items.label: Are BNM's conditions met?
items.detail: Correct form, signatures, need-to-know scope; if unsure, escalate to compliance.

cards.question: Which disclosure falls within one of the exceptions written into FSA section 133 itself?
options: A customer's statement sent to her employer, who asked politely
A summary of loan data that does not allow any particular customer to be identified
A list of high-value depositors shared with a property developer
cards.explanation: Section 133(2) excludes disclosures to BNM, non-identifying summaries and information already lawfully public from another source. An employer or developer request falls in none of these.

cards.title: Permitted disclosure to law enforcement
Handling a law enforcement request
cards.prompt: Put Daniel's steps for the caller's request in the right order.
steps: Decline to release anything over the phone and take the caller's details
Ask for the request in writing on the prescribed form
Check that it is specific and signed by an officer of the required rank
Pass it to the bank's designated team for verification and approval
Disclose only the information specified, on a need-to-know basis
Record what was disclosed, to whom and on what basis

cards.title: Real case: BNM enforcement action against CIMB Bank Berhad
cards.caption: Source: BNM Enforcement Action Publication Notice 02/2019. BNM took into account voluntary reporting of the incidents and immediate remedial steps.

items.label: When the incidents occurred
items.detail: Customer information of CIMB Bank was disclosed to third parties without authorisation.

items.label: Compound offered
items.detail: For offences of unauthorised disclosure under FSA section 133(1).

items.label: Administrative monetary penalty
items.detail: For breaching the standards in BNM's customer information policy document.

items.label: Year of BNM's actions
items.detail: Actions taken on 22 February and 17 May 2019; notice published by BNM on 27 May 2023.

cards.title: Real case: what the CIMB action teaches
Inside the Vault Room
cards.setting: Consumer Conduct office, Kuala Lumpur. Video call with Johor Bahru.

lines.text: The 'inspector' never sent anything in writing. Compliance thinks it was a social engineering attempt.
And yesterday a contractor photographed a screen with customer details in the call centre. He said it was for an IT ticket.
The MCIPD document names that exact risk: staff photographing screens or documents. Banks can restrict personal devices in high-risk areas like call centres.
Kavitha, escalate it now under the breach procedure. If it might cause significant harm or involve many customers, BNM must be told immediately.
On it. And I'll check the vendor's own training records too.

cards.title: A breach on a Friday afternoon
